transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I guess what brings me in is that I got myself really overextended with the historical society fundraiser. I sort of took it on like I could run the whole thing myself, even though that was never really realistic.

I started designing quilts for it, and then I was calling volunteers, making schedules, setting up all these little timelines and lists, and promising people deadlines that… looking back, I really couldn’t possibly meet. At the time it felt like I could just organize it all if I kept pushing, but it got to be a lot. More than a lot, honestly.
During this time, were you needing much less sleep than usual?

Yes. For a while there I was hardly sleeping at all, at least compared to what’s normal for me. I’d go to bed late because I was working on the quilt designs or rewriting some volunteer list, and then I’d wake up after just a few hours and feel like, well, I guess I’m up, might as well get started. It didn’t feel terrible at first, which is the strange part. I’d wake up with my mind already going—thinking about fabric, or who I needed to call, or some schedule I wanted to fix—and I’d just get right into it.

There were mornings I was up early enough that it felt almost ridiculous, like I should still be asleep, but I’d be ready to sew or make phone calls as soon as I thought people might be awake. And now it’s sort of flipped around. Now I’ll lie there awake worrying about everything I didn’t finish or said I’d do, or I sleep late and still wake up feeling worn out, like I didn’t really rest.
During that time, did you feel unusually euphoric or unusually cheerful?

Yes… yes, I did. At the beginning especially, I felt almost glowing. That sounds dramatic, but that’s really what it was like. I’d have an idea for a quilt pattern or some way to arrange the fundraiser pieces, and it felt brilliant to me, like every thought I had was the exact right one.

I was cheerful in this very revved-up way, like I was sure everything was going to come together because I could see it all so clearly in my head. But it wasn’t just pleasant cheerfulness. If someone questioned me or even gently suggested I slow down or rethink something, I got snappish. I’d feel like they were in the way, like they didn’t understand how important it was or how well I had it figured out. Looking back, I can see I was more irritable than I wanted to admit at the time.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day, or lost interest in almost everything?

Yes… I think so. I mean, what I notice most is that I just don’t care about things I normally care about. I used to love going out and checking my garden, seeing what was coming up, fussing over the little plants, looking through seed catalogs and marking things I wanted to try. And with quilting, I usually have ideas stacked up in my head—colors, patterns, entries I want to work on, all of that.

But lately I’ll just sit there and look at the fabric, or flip through the seed catalogs, and there’s just… nothing much there. It doesn’t spark anything. I don’t feel excited or even especially interested. It’s like I know those are supposed to be “my things,” but they feel far away from me.
During that revved-up period, did your behavior cause serious problems in your life, like major trouble at work, socially, or financially?

Yes… it did. I mean, I’m not working, so it wasn’t like I got in trouble at a job, but it definitely caused problems at home and with the historical society. I had taken on all these things—committees, lists, calls, organizing pieces, saying I’d handle this and that—and at first I was so sure I could do it all. I really believed I was being helpful.

But then I stopped actually keeping up with what I’d promised. People were waiting on me for answers or materials or decisions, and I just… I couldn’t face them. I’d see a name pop up or think about someone asking where something was, and I’d avoid it. My husband ended up having to step in more than he should have. He’s been keeping the house routines going, the meals and bills and just the regular things I usually help with, and he’s also had to deal with people from the historical society because I couldn’t bring myself to talk to them.

It’s embarrassing, honestly. I made such a big show of being able to handle everything, and then he was the one left smoothing it over.
